findings.description: No server_side_encryption_configuration block is defined, so objects in this bucket (including seeded vendor data) are stored without enforced SSE-KMS/SSE-S3 encryption.
The bucket omits an ACL and any aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, so it defaults to no explicit private setting and nothing prevents a future public ACL or bucket policy from exposing its contents.
No logging block is configured, so reads and writes to this data bucket are not recorded, hindering detection and forensic investigation of unauthorized access.
Versioning is disabled while force_destroy is true, so objects can be permanently overwritten or deleted (e.g. by ransomware or an attacker covering tracks) with no recoverable prior version.
This ledger export bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving sensitive financial export data unencrypted at rest.
No logging block is configured for the ledger bucket, so access to sensitive financial data is not auditable.
Versioning is not enabled and force_destroy is true, so ledger export objects can be irreversibly deleted or tampered with.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is associated with the bucket; the private ACL alone does not prevent a later bucket policy or ACL change from exposing the data publicly.
The model artifacts bucket defines versioning and logging but no server-side encryption configuration, so artifacts are stored unencrypted.
The bucket lacks an aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource, so public ACLs or policies are not centrally blocked.
No server_side_encryption_configuration is set, so runbooks (which commonly contain internal hostnames, procedures, and occasionally secrets) are stored unencrypted at rest.
No logging block is configured, so access to operational runbooks is not recorded for audit or incident response.
The bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, leaving it open to accidental public exposure via ACL or policy changes.
The centralized audit/log bucket does not log access to itself, so tampering with or exfiltration of audit logs would go unrecorded.
The audit log bucket uses the log-delivery-write ACL but has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, so nothing structurally prevents public exposure of audit logs.

A vendor roster spreadsheet is uploaded with no kms_key_id or server_side_encryption argument into a bucket that also lacks default encryption, so this potentially sensitive third-party data is stored in plaintext.
